title: Speed: distillation, caching, compile, fewer steps

questions.q: What does the formula give for Heun, 20 steps, CFG 7?
questions.why: 20 steps × 2 calls per step × 2 for CFG. It is the round figure: sample_heun's last step to sigma 0 makes one call, so the real count on such a schedule is 78.

questions.q: Why does CFG 1 run about twice as fast as CFG 7?
options: sampling_function drops the second conditioning when CFG is 1
Steps are skipped at low CFG
questions.answer: sampling_function drops the second conditioning when CFG is 1
questions.why: With one prediction needed, the unconditional call is left out.

questions.q: Which lever is a property of the weights, not a ComfyUI feature?
questions.why: Core only runs distilled weights. The training happened elsewhere.

questions.q: What is different between the node cache and a step cache?
options: The node cache reuses exact results, a step cache approximates inside a run
They are two names for one thing
A step cache only works on a CPU
The node cache changes the picture
questions.answer: The node cache reuses exact results, a step cache approximates inside a run
questions.why: Same inputs give the same output for the node cache. A step cache reuses a change it expects to be close.

questions.q: In the lab, Heun with 4 steps and Euler with 8 steps both make 8 calls. What does that show?
options: Compare solvers by calls, and Heun's error was far smaller on this toy
Heun is always better on every model
questions.answer: Compare solvers by calls, and Heun's error was far smaller on this toy
questions.why: 0.00637 against 0.04246 on a smooth toy problem. A real model may differ.

questions.q: You test torch.compile. What do you leave out of your timing?
options: The first run, which includes compiling
questions.answer: The first run, which includes compiling
questions.why: Compilation happens once, so time what repeats, and also time the same graph without the node.
